name: Colin Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for doing this, Colin. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or parties. It's all confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say out loud and what you really think. What does a normal day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work in the contact centre of a package holiday company. People ring to book holidays, change flights, add bags, or complain because the hotel pool was green. I've been there about fourteen months. The booking system is ancient, all green screens and codes, and I still have to look things up on a sheet stuck to my monitor.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's good about it, and what wears you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The good bit is when a couple rings for their honeymoon and you find them a room with a sea view. The hard bit is summer, when flights get cancelled and you've got a hundred people waiting and nothing to offer them. My team leader says I'm too slow on rebookings, which is fair, I panic with the codes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds about right to me, honestly. Most new tech at our place is a let-down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, it's like the self-check-in kiosks at airports, half of them don't work. At work I'd joke about it. I don't post much, maybe a meme in the group chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still be a bit nervous, because travel firms go under all the time. Last year they shut the team that handled cruises and moved the work to the website. AI or no AI, the company squeezes us every winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay put and get faster on rebookings, maybe ask the trainer for a refresher on the codes. I'd keep saving, I've got about three months' worth, and I'd keep using the AI thing now and then for writing complaint replies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not because of AI, because of the winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens in winter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bookings drop and the hours drop with them. Last January they cut overtime and asked for volunteers to take unpaid leave. My flatmate Sam and I were splitting the rent to the penny.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How did you get through it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ate a lot of pasta and didn't go out. I'd do the same again. It's annoying, but it's normal in travel, everyone knows that.

say: I'd joke it's like **airport kiosks**, half of them never work.
I'd post a **meme** in the group chat, nothing more.
think: Travel firms **go under** all the time, AI or not.
The company already moved the **cruise team's** work onto the website.
do: Ask the trainer for a **refresher** on rebooking codes.
Keep his **three months** of savings and keep adding.
Use the **AI tool** now and then for complaint replies.
feel: **Uneasy** about the winter slump, not about AI.
S0.quote: Travel firms go under all the time. Last year they shut the team that handled cruises and moved the work to the website.
fieldNote: His worry is **seasonal hours** and a shaky industry, already there without AI.
He uses AI **occasionally** and without strong feelings either way.
He shares **rent** with a flatmate and budgets tightly every winter.

steps.text: Ask the trainer for a refresher on the rebooking codes
Keep adding to his three months of savings before winter
Use the AI tool for drafting complaint replies

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Booking and answering customers. That's my whole job, in two words.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it makes sense for the company, people book holidays on their phones anyway. I'd probably say we'll have to move with it. I'm not going to stand outside with a placard about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think they'll cut the phone team by half and keep the ones who handle the complicated stuff. I'm not one of those yet. I'm not the worst, but I'm not safe either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get good at the AI tools the company brings in, once I've seen the others using them, so I'm useful. I'd keep my CV up to date and look at the airport, because the ground crew and check-in desks still need people. I'd push my savings up a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Like I'm standing on a platform and the train's coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the airport?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My cousin works baggage handling there and says they're always short. It's hands-on, shifts are early, but it pays about the same. And it's still travel, which I like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the company makes sense. Is anybody to blame here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. The company's not evil, it's just doing what's cheaper. If I owned it I'd probably do the same, I just wish they'd give us more warning.

say: I'd say it **makes sense** because people book holidays on their phones.
I'd say we'll have to **move with it**, not protest.
think: They'll cut the **phone team by half** and keep the complex-case agents.
I'm **not safe**, because I'm not one of those yet.
do: Learn the company's **AI tools** once colleagues are using them.
Update his CV and look at **airport ground jobs**.
Push savings a bit **higher** than three months.
feel: **Anxious**, like standing on a platform as the train comes.
S1.quote: The company's not evil, it's just doing what's cheaper. If I owned it I'd probably do the same, I just wish they'd give us more warning.
fieldNote: His **centre** outlook shows: he blames nobody and wants fair warning.
He'd adopt AI tools **after others** prove them, fitting his steady style.
His cousin's **baggage handling** job gives him a concrete hands-on fallback.

steps.text: Learn the company's new AI booking tools once colleagues use them
Apply for baggage handling or check-in jobs at the airport
Raise savings above three months of rent and bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's frightening. I'd still be learning the codes when it hit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say nobody's ready for this, not the company, not the government, not me. I'd say it to my mates at football and we'd probably all just stare at our drinks. I might share something online saying the government needs a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my job's gone, probably in a year. Booking holidays is pure thinking work. The airport baggage idea buys me about three years until robots come in 2031, and after that I don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go for the airport job straight away, before everyone else from every call centre tries the same. I'd cut out football subs and nights out. If it got tight, I'd move back to my parents' town, where rents are half what they are here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. My stomach drops a bit just thinking about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your flatmate, Sam?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to get his notice in on his warehouse job before they automate that too. Then we'd probably have a long talk about whether we keep the flat. Neither of us could cover it alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The football, then the takeaways, then the car. I'd keep the phone, because you need it for everything, including finding work.

say: I'd say nobody is **ready for this**, not firms, government or me.
I'd share posts saying the government needs **a plan**.
think: Booking holidays is **pure thinking work**, gone within a year.
Airport baggage work buys about **three years** until 2031.
do: Apply to the **airport** before other call centre staff do.
Move to his **parents' town** if rent gets too tight.
feel: **Alarmed**, with his stomach dropping at the thought.
S2.quote: Booking holidays is pure thinking work. The airport baggage idea buys me about three years until robots come in 2031, and after that I don't know.
fieldNote: He grasps the **robot delay** and uses it to choose airport work.
He knows **every call centre worker** would rush the same jobs.
Moving back to his **parents' town** is a real, practical option for him.

steps.text: Apply for airport baggage handling jobs straight away
Stop paying football subs and cut nights out
Move back to his parents' town if rent gets tight

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's better. That's enough to actually learn something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time if people start now. I'd tell the lads at work to stop waiting and get a trade. I'd say the government should help pay for courses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd keep this job two or three years, then it goes. Five years gives me time to train in something with my hands. My dad's mate fixes heating and air conditioning, and he's been saying for years he can't find young people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one I'd ask my dad's mate about an apprenticeship and do the evening certificate at the college. I'd keep the call centre job while I can, and use the AI tools there to look good until I leave. I'd save hard for the drop in pay while I'm an apprentice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but there's a path. That helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you take risks when things are proven. Is an apprenticeship proven enough?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heating's been around forever, and somebody has to climb into a loft and fix a boiler. Robots might do it one day, but not before 2034. That's proven enough for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your parents say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum would be pleased, she never liked me on the phones. My dad would say he told me so, because he wanted me to do a trade at sixteen.

say: I'd tell coworkers to **stop waiting** and get a trade.
I'd say the government should help **pay for courses**.
think: I'd keep this job **two or three years**, then it goes.

do: Ask his dad's friend about a **heating apprenticeship**.
Take the **evening certificate** at the college.
Save hard to cover the **apprentice pay drop**.
S3.quote: Somebody has to climb into a loft and fix a boiler. Robots might do it one day, but not before 2034.
fieldNote: Five years lets him pick a **trade** with a trusted contact.
He wants **proof** before risk, and an old trade counts as proof.
His father's **old advice** shapes his choice.

steps.text: Ask his dad's friend about a heating and air conditioning apprenticeship
Use the call centre's AI tools to keep his numbers up

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Okay. I'd be thirty-seven, probably still renting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and things will change in ways nobody expects. I'd say don't panic, but don't ignore it. I'd tell my mates the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd probably stay in the job for a while and see how it goes. I'd like to be further up by then, maybe a team leader. But I'd want a backup before 2036, because this job won't exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay in the job for now and watch what the company does. I'd start putting a bit into a pension and an index fund, so I'm not starting from zero. Maybe in two or three years I'd look at the heating apprenticeship.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit anxious, but I could live with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you want to be a team leader. Does that make sense if the job disappears?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe not, but team leaders might be the last ones out. They're the ones who'd run the bots. I'd try both, keep my options open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would tell you it's time to move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the summer rush came and they didn't hire temps. Every summer they bring in thirty students. When they stop doing that, I'd know.

feel: A bit **anxious**, but able to **live with it**.
S4.quote: Every summer they bring in thirty students. When they stop doing that, I'd know.
fieldNote: A decade lets him **delay** and hedge between promotion and a trade.

steps.text: Watch whether the company still hires summer temps

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it's too quick to learn a trade and everyone from every call centre would be chasing the same few jobs. What would help is paid apprenticeships for people my age, not just for school leavers.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the seasons. In travel, half my worry is just the winter. AI's a new problem stacked on top of an old one.

headlineQuote: In travel, half my worry is just the winter. AI's a new problem stacked on top of an old one.
portrait: Colin is 27 and takes **holiday bookings** at a package travel company's contact centre.
He's **slow on rebookings** and already lives with winter cuts in hours.
He's **pragmatic** and blames no one, only wishing firms gave more warning.
His fallback is **airport** ground work, then a **heating trade** if he has time.
He adopts tools **once proven** and watches hiring patterns for warning signs.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there's no time to learn a trade before everyone chases the same jobs.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid apprenticeships** open to people in their late twenties, not only school leavers.
